focus: Exodus 32 records Israel breaking the covenant at the foot of the mountain by worshiping a golden calf while Moses is still on the mountain. The chapter moves between the mountain and the camp: Moses intercedes and the LORD relents, Moses comes down and breaks the tablets, judgment falls, and Moses returns to the LORD to plead for the people’s forgiveness.

sections.title: Aaron Makes the Golden Calf and Proclaims a Feast
sections.summary: When Moses delays, the people ask Aaron to make gods to go before them, and he fashions a molded calf from their golden earrings. The people say, “This is your god, O Israel, that brought you out of the land of Egypt!” (Exodus 32:4), and Aaron builds an altar and proclaims, “Tomorrow is a feast to the LORD” (Exodus 32:5).

sections.title: Moses Intercedes and the LORD Relents
sections.summary: The LORD tells Moses that the people have corrupted themselves and that He will consume this stiff-necked people and make a great nation of Moses. Moses pleads for God’s name among the Egyptians and His oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and “the LORD relented from the harm which He said He would do to His people” (Exodus 32:14).

sections.title: Moses Breaks the Tablets and Destroys the Calf
sections.summary: Moses comes down with the two tablets, “the work of God” (Exodus 32:16), and when he sees the calf and the dancing, he breaks them at the foot of the mountain. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water, and makes Israel drink it.

sections.title: Aaron Excuses Himself
sections.summary: Moses asks Aaron what the people did to him that he brought so great a sin upon them. Aaron blames the people’s evil and claims that he cast their gold into the fire “and this calf came out” (Exodus 32:24).

sections.title: The Levites Answer Moses’ Call and Judgment Falls
sections.summary: Seeing the people unrestrained, Moses stands at the camp’s entrance and calls, “Whoever is on the LORD’s side—come to me!” (Exodus 32:26), and the sons of Levi gather to him. At his command they carry out judgment in the camp, about three thousand men fall, and Moses tells the Levites to consecrate themselves to the LORD.

sections.title: Moses Offers Himself for the People’s Forgiveness
sections.summary: Moses returns to the LORD and prays, “if You will forgive their sin—but if not, I pray, blot me out of Your book which You have written” (Exodus 32:32). The LORD answers that He will blot out whoever has sinned against Him, sends Moses to lead the people with His Angel going before them, and plagues the people because of the calf.

1.brief: When the people see that Moses delays coming down, they gather to Aaron and demand, “Come, make us gods that shall go before us,” since they do not know what has become of Moses. While Moses is still on the mountain, the people turn from waiting on God to demanding a visible god.
1.explain:
“Now when the people saw that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain,”

Moses has been on the mountain forty days (24:18). To the people, he seems to be delaying.

“the people gathered together to Aaron, and said to him, ‘Come, make us gods that shall go before us;”

They crowd around “Aaron” with a demand: “make us gods that shall go before us.” The LORD had been going before them in the pillar (13:21). Now they want a god they can see and control.

“for as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.”

They speak of “this Moses” with contempt. They credit him, not God, with bringing them out, and they give up on him. While Moses is still on the mountain, the people turn from waiting on God to demanding a visible god.
1.notes: The Hebrew word translated “gods” (elohim) can also mean God. The people may have meant a god or an image to represent God. The following verses suggest they intended to worship the LORD through the image (32:4–5).

2.brief: Aaron tells them to break off the golden earrings of their wives, sons, and daughters and bring them to him. Aaron goes along with the people’s demand instead of resisting it.
2.explain:
“And Aaron said to them, ‘Break off the golden earrings which are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me.”

Aaron does not refuse. He asks for “the golden earrings.” Aaron goes along with the people’s demand instead of resisting it.

3.brief: All the people break off their earrings and bring them to Aaron. The whole people take part in the rebellion.
3.explain:
“So all the people broke off the golden earrings which were in their ears, and brought them to Aaron.”

“All the people” gave. The gold God had provided from Egypt (12:35–36) is given to make an idol. The whole people take part in the rebellion.

4.brief: Aaron fashions the gold into a molded calf, and the people say, “This is your god, O Israel, that brought you out of the land of Egypt!” They credit an idol with the deliverance the LORD Himself accomplished.
4.explain:
“And he received the gold from their hand, and he fashioned it with an engraving tool, and made a molded calf.”

The narrator is clear about who made it. Aaron “received the gold,” “fashioned it with an engraving tool,” and “made a molded calf.” A calf or young bull was a common symbol of strength and fertility in the ancient Near East.

“Then they said, ‘This is your god, O Israel, that brought you out of the land of Egypt!”

The people credit the calf with their deliverance. They give an idol the credit for what the LORD Himself accomplished. Only weeks earlier God had said, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (20:2).
4.notes: Jeroboam later set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan with nearly the same words (1 Kings 12:28). Psalm 106:19–20 says Israel exchanged their glory for “the image of an ox that eats grass.”

5.brief: Aaron builds an altar before the calf and proclaims, “Tomorrow is a feast to the LORD.” Aaron tries to worship the LORD through an image, which the second commandment forbids.
5.explain:
“So when Aaron saw it, he built an altar before it.”

Aaron builds “an altar before it.” He organizes the worship.

“And Aaron made a proclamation and said, ‘Tomorrow is a feast to the LORD.”

Aaron calls it “a feast to the LORD,” using God’s covenant name. Aaron and the people try to worship the LORD through an image, which the second commandment forbids (20:4–5). The calf broke both the first and second commandments.

6.brief: The people rise early, offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, and sit down to eat and drink and rise up to play. Israel’s feast before the calf mimics true worship and turns into revelry.
6.explain:
“Then they rose early on the next day, offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings;”

The people offer “burnt offerings” and “peace offerings,” imitating true worship.

“and the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.”

The feast turns to revelry. “To play” describes celebration that may include immoral behavior. Israel’s feast before the calf mimics true worship and turns into revelry.
6.notes: Paul quotes this verse as a warning to the church: “do not become idolaters as were some of them” (1 Corinthians 10:7).

7.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “Go, get down! For your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have corrupted themselves.” God sees the corruption below and sends Moses down at once.
7.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Go, get down!”

God sees what is happening and orders Moses down at once.

“For your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have corrupted themselves.”

God calls them “your people whom you brought out.” It is as though God distances Himself from them. They “have corrupted themselves,” acting ruinously.

8.brief: The LORD says they have quickly turned aside from His way, made a molded calf, worshiped and sacrificed to it, and credited it with bringing them out of Egypt. Their covenant breach comes almost immediately after they promised obedience.
8.explain:
“They have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them.”

They “turned aside quickly.” Only forty days after promising, “All that the LORD has said we will do” (24:7), they have broken the covenant.

“They have made themselves a molded calf, and worshiped it and sacrificed to it, and said, ‘This is your god, O Israel, that brought you out of the land of Egypt!”

God repeats their words. He knows exactly what they did and said. Their covenant breach comes almost immediately after they promised obedience.

9.brief: The LORD says, “I have seen this people, and indeed it is a stiff-necked people!” God names their stubborn resistance to Him.
9.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘I have seen this people, and indeed it is a stiff-necked people!”

God calls Israel “a stiff-necked people.” The picture is of an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke. God names their stubborn resistance to Him.
9.notes: Stephen used the same charge against the council: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears!” (Acts 7:51).

10.brief: The LORD says, “Now therefore, let Me alone, that My wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them,” and offers to make a great nation from Moses. God’s holy anger is real, and His words open the way for Moses to intercede.
10.explain:
“Now therefore, let Me alone, that My wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them.”

God’s anger is real. He tells Moses, “let Me alone.” Yet by saying this to Moses, God opens the way for Moses to intercede. God’s holy anger is real, and His words invite Moses to stand in the gap.

“And I will make of you a great nation.”

God offers to start over with Moses, as He had with Abraham (Genesis 12:2). Moses refuses the offer.
10.notes: Psalm 106:23 says God would have destroyed Israel if “Moses His chosen one” had not stood before Him in the breach.

11.brief: Moses pleads with the LORD, asking why His wrath should burn against “Your people whom You have brought out of the land of Egypt” with great power. Moses reminds God that Israel is His own people whom He redeemed.
11.explain:
“Then Moses pleaded with the LORD his God, and said:”

Moses “pleaded,” literally sought the face of the LORD.

“LORD, why does Your wrath burn hot against Your people whom You have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?”

God had called them “your people” (32:7). Moses calls them “Your people whom You have brought out.” Moses reminds God that Israel is His own people whom He redeemed by His power.

12.brief: Moses asks why the Egyptians should say that God brought Israel out only to destroy them, and he pleads, “Turn from Your fierce wrath, and relent from this harm to Your people.” Moses appeals to the honor of God’s name among the nations.
12.explain:
“Why should the Egyptians speak, and say, ‘He brought them out to harm them, to kill them in the mountains, and to consume them from the face of the earth’?”

Moses’ second argument concerns God’s name among the nations. If God destroys Israel, Egypt will say He brought them out only to kill them. God’s reputation is at stake.

“Turn from Your fierce wrath, and relent from this harm to Your people.”

Moses asks God to “relent,” to change course from the judgment He announced. Moses appeals to the honor of God’s name among the nations.

13.brief: Moses asks God to remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, to whom He swore by Himself to multiply their descendants and give them the land forever. Moses appeals to God’s own oath to the fathers.
13.explain:
“Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Your servants, to whom You swore by Your own self, and said to them,”

Moses’ third argument is God’s own oath. God “swore” by Himself to the fathers (Genesis 22:16–17).

“I will multiply your descendants as the stars of heaven; and all this land that I have spoken of I give to your descendants, and they shall inherit it forever.”

God promised many descendants and the land forever. Moses appeals to God’s own oath to the fathers.

14.brief: “So the LORD relented from the harm which He said He would do to His people.” God truly responds to Moses’ intercession, consistent with His faithful character.
14.explain:
“So the LORD relented from the harm which He said He would do to His people.”

God responds to Moses’ prayer. He “relented” from the disaster He had announced. This does not mean God was caught by surprise or changed His character. His relenting is consistent with His faithful, merciful nature (34:6–7). Within His unchanging purposes, God has chosen to make prayer matter. He truly responds to His people’s requests.
14.notes: Scripture says both that God does not change His mind like a man (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29) and that He relents in response to repentance and intercession (Jeremiah 18:7–10; Jonah 3:10).

15.brief: Moses turns and goes down the mountain with the two tablets of the Testimony in his hand, written on both sides. Moses carries God’s covenant toward a people who have already broken it.
15.explain:
“And Moses turned and went down from the mountain, and the two tablets of the Testimony were in his hand.”

Moses goes down carrying “the two tablets.”

“The tablets were written on both sides; on the one side and on the other they were written.”

They were written “on both sides.” Moses carries God’s covenant toward a people who have already broken it.

16.brief: “Now the tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God.” The narrator stresses that what Moses carries came directly from God.
16.explain:
“Now the tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God engraved on the tablets.”

The narrator stresses that these were “the work of God” and “the writing of God.” What Moses carries came directly from God.

17.brief: When Joshua hears the shouting, he tells Moses, “There is a noise of war in the camp.” Joshua mistakes the sound of the feast for battle.
17.explain:
“And when Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted,”

“Joshua” had waited partway up the mountain (24:13). He hears noise from the camp.

“he said to Moses, ‘There is a noise of war in the camp.”

As a military leader (17:9), Joshua assumes it is battle. Joshua mistakes the sound of the feast for war.

18.brief: Moses answers that it is neither the shout of victory nor the cry of defeat, “But the sound of singing I hear.” Moses recognizes the sound of revelry before he sees the calf.
18.explain:
“But he said: ‘It is not the noise of the shout of victory, Nor the noise of the cry of defeat,”

Moses answers in a short poem. It is neither a victory shout nor a cry of defeat.

“But the sound of singing I hear.”

It is “singing.” Moses recognizes the sound of revelry before he sees the calf.

19.brief: When Moses sees the calf and the dancing, his anger burns, and he throws down the tablets and breaks them at the foot of the mountain. The broken tablets show that the covenant has been broken.
19.explain:
“So it was, as soon as he came near the camp, that he saw the calf and the dancing.”

Moses sees for himself “the calf and the dancing.”

“So Moses’ anger became hot, and he cast the tablets out of his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain.”

Moses throws down the tablets and breaks them “at the foot of the mountain,” where Israel had pledged to keep the covenant (24:4–8). The broken tablets show that the covenant has been broken.

20.brief: Moses burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water, and makes Israel drink it. The idol is utterly destroyed, and the people are made to bear its consequences.
20.explain:
“Then he took the calf which they had made, burned it in the fire, and ground it to powder;”

Moses destroys the idol. He burns it, grinds it “to powder.” The god they credited with their rescue cannot save itself.

“and he scattered it on the water and made the children of Israel drink it.”

He scatters the powder on the water and makes Israel “drink it.” The people are made to bear the consequences of their idol.
20.notes: Deuteronomy 9:21 adds that Moses threw the dust into the brook that came down from the mountain.

21.brief: Moses asks Aaron, “What did this people do to you that you have brought so great a sin upon them?” Moses holds Aaron responsible for leading the people into sin.
21.explain:
“And Moses said to Aaron, ‘What did this people do to you that you have brought so great a sin upon them?”

Moses confronts “Aaron.” He asks what the people did to make Aaron lead them into “so great a sin.” Moses holds Aaron responsible.

22.brief: Aaron tells Moses not to be angry, saying, “You know the people, that they are set on evil.” Aaron shifts the blame to the people.
22.explain:
“So Aaron said, ‘Do not let the anger of my lord become hot.”

Aaron begins by trying to calm Moses.

“You know the people, that they are set on evil.”

Then he blames the people for their evil bent. Aaron shifts the blame to the people.

23.brief: Aaron repeats the people’s demand for gods to go before them because they did not know what had become of Moses. Aaron presents himself as simply responding to pressure.
23.explain:
“For they said to me, ‘Make us gods that shall go before us; as for this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.”

Aaron repeats the people’s demand accurately. He presents himself as simply responding to pressure.

24.brief: Aaron claims he told them to break off their gold, cast it into the fire, “and this calf came out.” His account hides his own workmanship, which verse 4 plainly reports.
24.explain:
“And I said to them, ‘Whoever has any gold, let them break it off.”

Aaron admits he asked for the gold.

“So they gave it to me, and I cast it into the fire, and this calf came out.”

Then he claims, “and this calf came out,” as if by itself. Exodus 32:4 reports that Aaron fashioned it with a tool. His account hides his own workmanship.
24.notes: Deuteronomy 9:20 says the LORD was very angry with Aaron and would have destroyed him, but Moses prayed for Aaron also.

25.brief: Moses sees that the people are unrestrained, “for Aaron had not restrained them,” to their shame among their enemies. The rebellion is out of control and dishonors Israel before the nations.
25.explain:
“Now when Moses saw that the people were unrestrained”

The people are “unrestrained,” out of control. The word can mean let loose or running wild.

“(for Aaron had not restrained them, to their shame among their enemies),”

The narrator again names Aaron’s failure. The rebellion dishonors Israel “among their enemies.”

26.brief: Moses stands at the entrance of the camp and calls, “Whoever is on the LORD’s side—come to me!” and all the sons of Levi gather to him. Moses calls for a clear choice of loyalty, and the Levites answer.
26.explain:
“then Moses stood in the entrance of the camp, and said, ‘Whoever is on the LORD’s side—come to me!”

Moses calls for a clear choice: “Whoever is on the LORD’s side—come to me!” No one can stay neutral.

“And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves together to him.”

Moses’ own tribe answers the call.

27.brief: Moses tells the Levites that the LORD God of Israel commands them to take their swords and go through the camp, killing even brother, companion, and neighbor. The command is a one-time judgment at a moment of open rebellion against the covenant just made.
27.explain:
“And he said to them, ‘Thus says the LORD God of Israel:”

Moses speaks with God’s authority.

“Let every man put his sword on his side, and go in and out from entrance to entrance throughout the camp, and let every man kill his brother, every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.”

The Levites are to go through the camp with the sword, sparing no one because of family ties. This was a one-time judgment at a moment of open rebellion against the covenant just made (24:3–8). The golden calf was high treason against the LORD.

28.brief: The sons of Levi do as Moses commands, and about three thousand men fall that day. The judgment is carried out under Moses’ authority and supplies no pattern for religious violence among God’s people.
28.explain:
“So the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses.”

The Levites act “according to the word of Moses,” not from personal zeal.

“And about three thousand men of the people fell that day.”

About “three thousand men” died. The judgment was carried out under Moses’ authority as God’s appointed leader, to stop the rebellion and preserve the covenant people. This judgment belongs to a unique moment in Israel’s covenant history and supplies no pattern for religious violence. Under the new covenant God Himself executes such judgment, and He does not authorize believers to take up the sword for Him (John 18:36; 2 Corinthians 10:4). God’s judgment on Ananias and Sapphira at the birth of the church shows a similar seriousness, and there God Himself carried it out (Acts 5:1–11).

29.brief: Moses tells the Levites, “Consecrate yourselves today to the LORD,” that He may bless them, because each one stood against even son and brother. The Levites’ loyalty to the LORD sets them apart for His service.
29.explain:
“Then Moses said, ‘Consecrate yourselves today to the LORD,”

Moses tells the Levites to “consecrate” themselves, literally fill your hands, the expression used for installing priests (28:41).

“that He may bestow on you a blessing this day, for every man has opposed his son and his brother.”

They put loyalty to God above family ties. The Levites’ loyalty to the LORD sets them apart for His service. Later they were given the care of the tabernacle (Numbers 3:5–13; Deuteronomy 33:8–9).

30.brief: The next day Moses tells the people, “You have committed a great sin,” and says he will go up to the LORD; perhaps he can make atonement. Moses names the sin plainly and still seeks forgiveness for them.
30.explain:
“Now it came to pass on the next day that Moses said to the people, ‘You have committed a great sin.”

Moses names the sin plainly: “a great sin.”

“So now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin.”

Moses will go back to God. “Perhaps” shows he does not presume. He seeks forgiveness for the people.

31.brief: Moses returns to the LORD and confesses, “Oh, these people have committed a great sin, and have made for themselves a god of gold!” Moses does not excuse the sin when he prays.
31.explain:
“Then Moses returned to the LORD and said, ‘Oh, these people have committed a great sin,”

Moses confesses the sin to God without excuse.

“and have made for themselves a god of gold!”

He names it exactly: “a god of gold.” Moses does not excuse the sin when he prays.

32.brief: Moses prays, “Yet now, if You will forgive their sin—but if not, I pray, blot me out of Your book which You have written.” Moses offers himself for the people, a willingness that points toward the Son who gave Himself for His people.
32.explain:
“Yet now, if You will forgive their sin—”

Moses asks God to “forgive.” The sentence breaks off, as if Moses cannot finish.

“but if not, I pray, blot me out of Your book which You have written.”

If God will not forgive them, Moses asks to be blotted out of “Your book,” the record of the living or of God’s people. Moses offers himself for the people. Moses could not bear the people’s sin himself. Christ did, giving Himself for His people, and He lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25–27).
32.notes:
Paul expressed a similar willingness to be accursed for the sake of his people (Romans 9:3).

Scripture speaks of a book of the living (Psalm 69:28) and the Lamb’s Book of Life (Revelation 21:27).

33.brief: The LORD answers, “Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot him out of My book.” God holds each sinner accountable for his own sin.
33.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot him out of My book.”

God refuses Moses’ offer. “Whoever has sinned against Me” will bear it. One sinner cannot bear another’s guilt. God holds each sinner accountable for his own sin.

34.brief: God tells Moses to lead the people to the place He spoke of, for “My Angel shall go before you,” yet He will punish them for their sin in His time. God continues to guide Israel while warning of judgment.
34.explain:
“Now therefore, go, lead the people to the place of which I have spoken to you.”

God tells Moses to keep leading the people toward the land.

“Behold, My Angel shall go before you.”

God will send “My Angel” before them (23:20).

“Nevertheless, in the day when I visit for punishment, I will visit punishment upon them for their sin.”

But judgment will still come in God’s time. God continues to guide Israel while warning of judgment.

35.brief: “So the LORD plagued the people because of what they did with the calf which Aaron made.” The chapter ends with God’s judgment and names Aaron as the calf’s maker.
35.explain:
“So the LORD plagued the people because of what they did with the calf which Aaron made.”

God sends a plague. The narrator names the calf as the one “which Aaron made.” Aaron’s excuse (32:24) is not accepted. The chapter ends with judgment and leads into the question of whether the LORD will still go with Israel (33:1–3).
